key_facts: The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held a virtual meeting with various members presenting petitions.

A petition from the Canadian Perinatal Mental Health Collaborative calls for a national perinatal mental health strategy, citing 20% of women and 10% of men suffer from perinatal mental illness in Canada.

A petition related to cystic fibrosis asks the government to rescind amendments to the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board to ensure access to the drug Trikafta, which is effective for 90% of CF sufferers.
Petitioners highlight that nearly five million Canadians lack a regular family doctor, urging the government to collaborate with provinces and territories to solve this crisis.
A petition criticizes the Liberal government's approach to firearms legislation, calling for cancellation of plans to confiscate legally owned firearms and focusing on gang-related violence.
Petitioners oppose open-net salmon farming expansion in Nova Scotia due to environmental concerns and call for compliance with Bill C-68 and species-at-risk legislation.
Petitioners demand immediate halting of the Coastal GasLink project on Wet'suwet'en territory, emphasizing the need for nation-to-nation talks and adherence to UNDRIP.
A petition requests airlines to provide full refunds for cancelled flights due to the pandemic before receiving any government financial assistance.
Federal workers were instructed to prioritize speed over fraud detection in distributing pandemic benefits, with 200,000 applications flagged as potentially fraudulent.
The Prime Minister emphasized that the government will retroactively address fraud after ensuring timely distribution of support during the crisis.
The Large Employer Emergency Financing Facility includes conditions against tax evasion and avoidance but allows companies to legally benefit from tax havens.
There are concerns about high interchange fees charged by credit card companies, with petitioners asking the government to cap these fees at 0.3%, similar to Europe and Australia.
Single parents who lost spousal and child support due to the pandemic are not eligible for CERB, prompting a call for correction.
Service Canada has experienced delays in processing mail submissions, including unopened documents sent two months ago.
Farmers in Canada have been affected by the Iver Johnson rifle ban, which critics argue targets law-abiding citizens rather than addressing illegal weapons.
Seniors are being supported with a one-time payment of up to $500, but there are concerns about inadequate measures and delayed responses to their needs.
The government faces criticism for its handling of PPE procurement, with some provinces reporting shortages and issues with faulty or expired equipment.
Fishermen in the lobster industry are experiencing significant market losses due to the pandemic and require targeted support, as they are not eligible for existing programs like the wage subsidy.
Health Canada has not received an application for Trikafta, a life-saving drug for cystic fibrosis patients, despite calls for expedited approval.
The tourism sector is severely impacted by the pandemic, especially ferry services connecting Nova Scotia to Maine, requiring federal support to survive and recover.

Quebec representatives raised concerns about wealth inequality, noting CEOs earn 227 times more than average workers, and questioned whether executive compensation caps would be imposed on firms receiving crisis support.
The government announced liquidity measures for the oil and gas sector, including $500 million for large-cap companies, following prolonged delays.
Proposals for universal pharmacare were reiterated, highlighting the vulnerability of millions of Canadians who lost prescription coverage when they lost jobs.
Long-term care facilities face a crisis with poor conditions and high mortality rates, prompting demands for national standards and federal funding tied to enforcement.
Questions arose regarding transparency and accountability in government decision-making, including the Harrington Cottage renovation and leaks of pre-market economic data.
The Coastal GasLink pipeline received a $500 million loan from Export Development Canada, raising concerns about fairness compared to past forestry sector support.

Small businesses struggling with rent relief and PPE access during reopening were advised to rely on provincial involvement for landlord cooperation and federal-provincial coordination for PPE availability.
Concerns were raised about the CERB repayment threshold, where even minor earnings over $1,000 could result in losing the entire benefit, prompting reassurances of individualized support.
